summary.one_line: A profitable, export-heavy (95%) Madhya Pradesh maker of propeller shafts and driveline parts. About two-thirds of the fresh money goes into real capex and debt repayment. But revenue is growing only about 6% a year, part of the FY26 profit jump came from currency, half of product sales go to a US market under a 25% tariff, and the promoter-group governance record is weak. Our call is avoid at the IPO.
bull_points: Vertically integrated: die-making, forging, heat treatment, machining, balancing and testing are all done in-house across three Madhya Pradesh plants, and the portfolio has more than 5,000 SKUs (S1, S7).
Margins and returns have improved: EBITDA margin rose from 23.84% (FY24) to 27.66% (FY26), PAT from Rs 14.53 cr to Rs 26.16 cr, and RoCE from 15.07% to 19.01% (S1, S3, S7).

The company has been cutting debt and converts profit to cash reasonably well. Debt/equity fell from 1.43x (FY23) to 0.41x (FY26), and FY26 operating cash flow was Rs 29.41 cr against PAT of Rs 26.16 cr (S1, S3, S7).
Most of the issue is fresh money for the business: Rs 132.62 cr fresh vs Rs 18.09 cr OFS. About Rs 88 cr is earmarked for plant capex and subsidiary debt repayment (S3, S17).
The forging plant is running near full: Dewas utilisation was 87.87% in FY26, which supports adding forging capacity (S17).
bear_points: Growth is slow. Revenue from operations went from Rs 124.53 cr to Rs 139.94 cr over FY24-FY26, a CAGR of about 6% (S3, S6).
Roughly Rs 4.3 cr of the Rs 10.1 cr rise in FY26 pre-tax profit comes from swinging from a Rs 3.81 cr FX loss to a Rs 0.50 cr FX gain, and the exposure is completely unhedged (S7, S15).
The company is highly exposed to exports and the US. 95.39% of FY26 product sales were exports, the US alone was 51.28% of product sales, and US shipments face a 25% Section 232 tariff (S15, S21).

The promoter group has a poor governance record: 46 delayed ROC filings (one 3,771 days late), a pending FEMA compounding application, five criminal cases against promoter Mukesh Sangla, and a SEBI refusal to exempt the non-cooperating Yashwant Sangla group from disclosure (S11, S19, S20).
Rs 21.49 cr (about 17% of net worth) is invested in promoter-influenced Signet Industries, a listed plastics company, and the two companies also trade with each other (S14).
watch_points: Whether the planned Pithampur expansion (9 lakh to 18 lakh units) finds demand. The plant ran at only 74.70% utilisation in FY26 (S17).
What happens to US tariffs, and whether the US share of exports keeps falling (71.93% in FY24, 53.76% in FY26) (S15).
Working capital: net working capital days were about 233-263 over the reported periods, with inventory at about 128-137 days (S1).
How the pending RBI/FEMA compounding and ROC adjudications turn out, and whether the company files on time after listing (S19).
Final subscription by category on 25 September. Day-1 exchange data was not available when this was written (S26).

reasoning: The use of proceeds is reasonable, but it mainly helps the subsidiary. Of the roughly Rs 88 cr allocated to specific objects, Rs 68.08 cr goes into subsidiary Adroit Driveshafts (Pithampur capex plus loan repayment). That subsidiary earned Rs 127.82 cr of the group's Rs 139.94 cr FY26 revenue. It is still productive capex, not an exit: the OFS is only Rs 18.09 cr (S3, S16, S17).

There is no durable moat. The edges are in-house forging and a 12-18 month customer qualification cycle, but 62.45% of product sales go through distributors, the company has no long-term contracts, and it competes with much larger listed Indian peers and global driveline majors (S1, S8, S18, S22, S23).

The quality of growth does not support a premium story. Revenue compounded at about 6% over FY24-FY26, and around 40% of the FY26 pre-tax profit increase was an FX swing on unhedged exposure rather than an operating gain (S3, S7, S15).

Governance is the deciding negative. The record includes 46 late statutory filings (some years late), a pending FEMA compounding application, criminal and tax cases against a promoter, and a promoter-group relative who would not give SEBI the required undertakings. It also includes Rs 21.49 cr parked in a promoter-influenced listed company and promoter-group shares sold to Abakkus at Rs 90 a month before an IPO priced at Rs 126-134 (S11, S14, S19, S20, S28).

Concentration adds to the risk. About half of product sales depend on US demand under a 25% tariff, the top 10 customers bring in 60.86% of sales, the top 10 suppliers account for about 90% of purchases, and all plants are in one state (S1, S15, S18).

What would move the call to 'track': several listed quarters showing clean, on-time compliance, no further capital going into group companies (the Signet stake, S14), resolution of the pending FEMA and ROC matters (S19), and growth in the double digits without FX help, against about 6% in FY24-FY26 (S6, S15).

subsections.title: What Adroit makes and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Adroit makes propeller shafts (also called drive shafts or cardan shafts) and precision-machined torque-transmission components for vehicle and machinery drivelines. It sells them as complete assemblies, sub-assemblies or individual components, built to customer specifications. The portfolio has more than 5,000 SKUs. The company sells into automotive (mainly commercial vehicles plus a few passenger SUVs) and non-automotive uses such as defence, heavy and off-highway equipment and industrial machinery (S1). The business started as a partnership firm in 1966 and was incorporated as a company in 1995 (S1, S7).

Revenue comes from product sales, split into two lines: machined torque-transmission components (yokes, flanges, joint parts and similar) and finished propeller shaft assemblies. Machined components are still the larger line, but assemblies are growing as a share: from 23.74% of product sales in FY23 to 34.41% in FY25 and 37.62% in H1 FY26 (S1). That shift moves revenue toward higher-value complete assemblies.

blocks.caption: Product revenue mix (Rs million, restated; from the DRHP summary)

blocks.text: In FY26, product sales were Rs 127.11 cr, which 5paisa reports as 'revenue' of Rs 127.1 cr, while reported revenue from operations was Rs 139.94 cr (S3, S5, S21). That leaves about Rs 12.8 cr (around 9%) of operating revenue that is not product sales. The secondary sources we could read do not break this down. One summary of the RHP risk factors says the company relies on tax and export incentives (S6), so part of this may be export benefits. We could not confirm the composition, so treat it as an open question.

By end use, automotive applications were 74.54% of FY26 product sales (Rs 94.75 cr) and non-automotive 25.46% (Rs 32.36 cr) (S18). That is close to the 72.50% automotive share in FY25 (S1). For shaft makers, the long-run risk to automotive demand is electrification. Single-motor EV layouts often do without a long propeller shaft, though heavy commercial vehicles are further from that shift.

This is mostly an export aftermarket and Tier-1 supply business, not an OEM supplier. In FY26, distributors bought 62.45% of product sales (Rs 79.38 cr), Tier-1 driveline suppliers 32.86% (Rs 41.77 cr) and OEMs directly only 4.68% (Rs 5.96 cr). There were 153 distributors, 13 Tier-1 customers and 22 OEM customers (S18). Sales are on purchase orders with no long-term agreements (S1).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration and base (share of product sales)

blocks.text: Table sources: FY23-FY25 concentration and customer counts from the DRHP abridged prospectus (S1); FY26 figures and repeat-customer revenue from RHP-based summaries (S18). Concentration is falling as the customer count grows, but one customer still accounts for about a fifth of sales. Customers named in brokers' RHP summaries include Godrej & Boyce, BEML, VE Commercial Vehicles, Sandvik Mining and Oilgear India (S22). Those are mostly domestic or India-based names, though, and domestic sales were only 4.61% of the total. The large overseas distributors that drive revenue are not named in the sources we could access.

blocks.caption: Geographic mix of product sales (Rs crore)

blocks.text: Table sources: S15 and S21. After the US, the largest FY26 export markets were Colombia (Rs 14.09 cr, 11.62% of exports), Canada (Rs 10.76 cr, 8.88%), Australia (Rs 6.85 cr, 5.65%) and Mexico (Rs 4.33 cr, 3.57%) (S21). US sales fell in absolute terms, from Rs 75.15 cr in FY24 to Rs 65.18 cr in FY26 (S9). So the lower US share came partly from a shrinking US business, not only from growth elsewhere.

Production runs in sequence across three Madhya Pradesh sites. Dewas (the parent company) does die-making, forging, heat treatment and raw-material testing. Pithampur (subsidiary Adroit Driveshafts Pvt Ltd, ADPL) does precision machining, assembly, balancing and testing. Sanwer handles finishing of machined components (S1). The plants hold IATF 16949, ISO 9001, ISO 14001 and ISO 45001 certifications (S7). The group also has subsidiaries in Canada and the USA to support North American sales (S6).

Table source: S17. The Dewas forging shop is close to full, so expanding it is justified. Pithampur still has about 25% spare capacity and the plan is to double it. That will only pay off if demand grows much faster than the roughly 5% a year product sales have grown recently (S17, S21).

Suppliers are very concentrated. The top ten suppliers accounted for 88.09% of purchases in FY24, 90.41% in FY25 and 91.84% in H1 FY26, and they are described as a limited number of domestic suppliers of key raw materials (S1). The model looks like this: buy steel inputs in India, forge and machine in-house in Madhya Pradesh, then ship finished parts mostly to overseas distributors. That creates a long pipeline, which shows up in net working capital of about 233-263 days (S1).

In practice this is a Madhya Pradesh manufacturer selling replacement driveline parts to overseas distributors, with about half of product sales ending up in the US. All plants are in one state, most sales go overseas, and the main raw materials come from a handful of suppliers (S1, S15).

The DRHP's industry section relies on a commissioned CareEdge report. That report describes propeller shafts as a capital-intensive, technically demanding niche inside automotive and industrial driveline components, with multi-tier supply chains and long approval cycles. It names vehicle production, industrial and off-highway machinery, and demand for lightweight materials such as aluminium and alloys as growth drivers (S1). The DRHP summary we read does not quote a specific Indian market size.

Third-party estimates of the global market vary widely. Grand View Research puts the global propeller shaft market at USD 28.51 billion in 2023, growing at a 5.8% CAGR to 2030. Other houses quote figures an order of magnitude smaller, depending on how they define the market (S8). The reasonable conclusion is that this is a large, mature, mid-single-digit-growth market. Adroit's roughly USD 15 million of revenue is a tiny share of it, so market size is not what limits the company.

Broker summaries of the RHP say the industry section cites growth in the Indian auto component industry, defence indigenisation, the National Rail Plan 2030 and Dedicated Freight Corridor projects as tailwinds (S22, S23). Those are mostly domestic themes, while Adroit sells more than 95% abroad (S21). So much of the industry narrative describes a market the company barely serves today.

The RHP's listed-peer set is Hindustan Hardy, Talbros Engineering and GNA Axles (S22, S23). By FY25 revenue, Adroit (Rs 133.89 cr) is larger than Hindustan Hardy (Rs 81.45 cr) but much smaller than Talbros Engineering (Rs 446.09 cr) and GNA Axles (Rs 1,539.74 cr) (S23). Globally, driveline and propeller shaft supply is led by Dana, GKN Automotive, American Axle, Hyundai Wia and JTEKT (S8). These are the incumbents Adroit's distributor and Tier-1 customers can buy from, or compete against.

blocks.caption: Scale comparison with RHP peers (FY25 revenue only; valuation excluded by design)

blocks.text: Table source: S23. Adroit's niche is the export aftermarket: replacement shafts and components sold through overseas distributors, often in low volumes across many SKUs. That differs from GNA Axles' high-volume OEM axle-shaft business. The large SKU count (5,250 in FY26, up about 37% from FY24) points to a broad catalogue, not deep ties with OEM platforms (S7, S13).

Adroit has some real advantages. In-house forging is uncommon among small Indian shaft makers and gives it control over cost and lead time (S1, S9). Customer qualification takes 12-18 months or more, with audits and tooling investment, so a new supplier cannot easily replace an approved one at a Tier-1 or OEM account (S22). About 90% of revenue comes from repeat customers (S18).

Those are operating strengths, not a moat. Most sales (62.45%) go through distributors, who can and do switch sources on price. There are no long-term contracts (S1, S18). Adroit does not claim to be the only Indian maker, and we found no market-share or import-substitution claim in the documents. Listed Indian peers make similar products (S23). The 25% US Section 232 tariff also shows that Adroit's cost position can be offset by policy it does not control (S15).

Our judgement: no real moat. Adroit is a capable, certified, vertically integrated niche exporter with sticky but non-contractual customer relationships. Its advantages are cost and catalogue breadth, which competitors can replicate. They are not regulatory or technological barriers.

Table sources: FY23 from the DRHP summary (S1); FY24-FY26 from RHP-based summaries (S3, S7), which agree with the DRHP's FY24 and FY25 figures (S1); FX from S15. Revenue grew 20% in FY24, then 7.5% in FY25 and 4.5% in FY26, a two-year CAGR of about 6% (S6). Profit grew much faster than revenue. The margin gains in FY24 and FY26 did the work.

The FY26 profit jump needs a closer look. Pre-tax profit rose by about Rs 10.1 cr (from Rs 22.82 cr to Rs 32.90 cr), while total expenses fell from Rs 113.79 cr to Rs 110.14 cr even though revenue grew (S7). Moving from a Rs 3.81 cr FX loss in FY25 to a Rs 0.50 cr FX gain in FY26 accounts for about Rs 4.3 cr of that rise, roughly 40%. The company does no hedging at all (S15). Some of the remaining gain may come from the shift toward assemblies and better utilisation, but we could not confirm the cost-line detail from the full RHP. The FY26 margin of 27.66% should not be treated as the normal level.

The profit trend looks better than the operating trend. Revenue grew about 6% a year while PAT grew about 34% a year over FY24-FY26 (S6). Currency helped a lot, and currency can reverse just as easily.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, debt and working capital

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and efficiency (Rs crore unless stated)

blocks.text: Table sources: FY23-FY25 and H1 FY26 from the DRHP summary (S1); FY26 net worth, debt and ratios from S3, S6 and S7. Debt has fallen every year and gearing is now moderate. Secondary sources conflict on borrowing figures. Chittorgarh's and IndiaIPO's tables show 'total borrowing' of only Rs 16.29 cr (FY24) and Rs 8.32 cr (FY25), which looks like a single debt line. Groww shows 'outstanding borrowings' of Rs 68.98 cr, possibly at a later date (S3, S12, S13). We use the DRHP's total debt and the 0.41x FY26 debt/equity (about Rs 52.4 cr), because both are consistent with the reported net worth (S1, S6).

Working capital is the weak spot on the balance sheet. The business ties up about eight months of revenue in net working capital, with more than four months of inventory, which is typical of a many-SKU export catalogue business shipping by sea (S1). This is why growth absorbs cash, and it is one reason FY23 operating cash flow was negative.

One balance-sheet item has nothing to do with the core business: a Rs 21.49 cr investment in the equity and preference shares of Signet Industries, a promoter-influenced listed plastics company. That is about 17% of FY26 net worth, and it was Rs 24.58 cr in FY24 (S14). The promoters and governance section covers it in more detail.

blocks.caption: Operating cash flow vs PAT (Rs crore)

blocks.text: Table sources: FY23-H1 FY26 from S1; FY26 CFO from S7 and PAT from S3. Since FY24, reported profit has turned into cash, and there is no current mismatch between cash flow and profit. FY23 is the exception: operating cash flow was negative Rs 23.4 cr while financing inflow was Rs 35.2 cr. That was the year ADPL, bought from the promoters in 2022, was consolidated and working capital built up (S1, S16).

From FY24 to FY25, operating cash flow and small investing inflows went to repay financing: financing outflows were Rs 19.7 cr in FY24 and Rs 23.5 cr in FY25 (S1). That funded the deleveraging. The IPO now pays for the next round of capex rather than internal cash flow (S17).

Does the trend support the growth story? Only partly. Profitability, cash conversion and leverage have all improved. The top line has not accelerated, and the most recent margin step-up relied on FX. The IPO argument really depends on capacity additions producing sales growth that the last two years have not shown.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Offer structure at the Rs 134 upper band

blocks.text: Table source: S3. About 88% of the issue is fresh capital. The only seller is Mukesh Sangla HUF, part of the promoter group, which acquired its shares at a weighted average cost of Rs 3.65 per share (S1). The allocation is up to 50% QIB, at least 15% NII and at least 35% retail. The lot size is 111 shares, so the minimum retail application is Rs 14,874. Bidding runs 23-25 September 2026, allotment is on 28 September and listing on BSE and NSE is on 30 September. Choice Capital Advisors is the sole book-running lead manager and Bigshare Services is the registrar (S3).

Promoter and promoter-group holding falls from 96.10% before the issue to 71.86% after (S3). There were no outside shareholders at the DRHP stage (S1). In late August 2026, promoter-group companies Signet Impex and Signet Tradelinks sold 13.62 lakh shares (3.90% of capital) at Rs 90 per share. The buyers were Abakkus Venture Opportunities Fund (11.11 lakh shares, 3.18%), Chattisgarh Investments (0.64%) and one individual (S28). That price is 33% below the Rs 134 cap, one month before the IPO.

subsections.title: What the fresh money is for

blocks.caption: Objects of the issue (Rs crore)
rows: Machinery and equipment plus transport vehicle, Dewas forging facility (parent)
Investment in subsidiary ADPL for machinery and equipment plus transport vehicle, Pithampur
Investment in ADPL to repay or prepay its borrowings
General corporate purposes plus offer expenses
GCP capped at 25% of gross proceeds

blocks.text: Table sources: DRHP amounts from S1 (converted from Rs million); RHP amounts from S3, S6 and S22; deployment schedule from S17; balance from S24. The RHP raised every specified object by about 19% compared with the DRHP. Zerodha puts general corporate purposes at Rs 44.63 cr (34%) (S24). Since GCP cannot legally exceed 25% of gross proceeds (about Rs 33 cr) (S1), that Rs 44.63 cr must include offer expenses. We could not confirm the exact split between GCP and expenses.

The capex is linked to specific capacity: Dewas forging from 3,000 MT to 5,500 MT and Pithampur from 9 lakh to 18 lakh units (S17). The company has not signed definitive supply agreements for the machinery, and the quotes it has exclude freight, insurance and installation, so cost overruns are possible (S17). Spending runs over FY27-FY28, so the new capacity would contribute to revenue mainly from FY28-FY29.

subsections.title: What this means for the investment case

items: Almost all the money goes into the business. The OFS is only 12% of the issue, and the promoter-group seller is not cashing out a large stake (S3).

Most of the money goes to the subsidiary. Rs 68.08 cr of the Rs 87.99 cr for specified objects goes to ADPL, which produced Rs 127.82 cr of FY26 revenue and Rs 22.19 cr of PAT. ADPL is where the business actually operates (S16, S17).

Debt repayment of Rs 24.12 cr against FY26 consolidated debt of about Rs 52.4 cr would roughly halve group borrowing, assuming no new debt. ADPL's standalone debt/equity was already 1.07x in FY26, down from 2.16x (S7, S16).
Doubling Pithampur while it runs at about 75% utilisation is the main execution bet. The growth case depends on new demand appearing, especially outside the tariff-hit US market (S15, S17).

blocks.text: On objects alone the issue is reasonable. It is capex- and deleveraging-led, not an exit. The concerns are with the business's growth record and the governance around it, not with where the money goes.

blocks.caption: Promoters and key management
rows: Chairman and Managing Director; promoter (2.97% directly)
BSc, University of California; 18+ years in plastics manufacturing and torque transmission
No formal education; 40+ years trading commodities and polymers, 20+ years in plastics manufacturing, 8+ years in torque transmission; Managing Director of Signet Industries
BA, University of Indore; director of Signet Tradelinks for 20+ years
Shreya Trust, Shubhangi Trust, Swan Irrigation LLP

blocks.text: Table sources: S1, S10 and S12. The board has five members: the CMD, one non-executive promoter director and three independent directors (Surabhi Agrawal, Anirudha Chauhan and Narendra Kumar Maheshwari) (S1). The promoters' background is mainly in plastics and polymer trading through the Signet group. Mukesh Sangla's disclosed experience in torque transmission is only 8+ years, and Saurabh Sangla's 18+ years spans both plastics and torque transmission (S1). The summaries we read do not explain how the family's involvement lines up with the business's 1966 origin. The driveline business is not the promoters' main historical expertise.

Control is spread across many family vehicles. The six named promoters hold 48.70% and seven promoter-group entities hold 51.30%. These include Mukesh Sangla HUF, Signet Impex, Signet Tradelinks, Ornate Impex, Shree Balaji Starch and Chemicals LLP, Aishwarya Trust and Ananda Trust (S1). The RHP lists 27 promoter-group entities. Group company Kozzby International signed a non-compete agreement on 23 March 2026, a week before the DRHP was filed (S11). All promoter shares came from gifts and bonus issues, at nil cost (S1).

blocks.caption: Dealings with Signet Industries (a director has significant influence) (Rs crore)

blocks.text: Table source: S14. This is not a routine related-party section. Adroit, a driveline business, holds Rs 21.49 cr of equity and preference shares in Signet Industries, a listed plastics and micro-irrigation company where Mukesh Sangla is Managing Director (S10, S14). That is about 17% of Adroit's net worth. The preference shares are growing, which suggests accruing or reinvested value. Trading with Signet was also 7% of FY26 revenue from operations. The FY26 flows also include small rent received, and purchases and sales of used plant and equipment, including an extruder (S14). IPO shareholders are effectively also exposed to the promoters' other business.

The operating subsidiary ADPL was bought from Mukesh and Saurabh Sangla in 2022: 99.87% for Rs 7.50 cr at face value (S16). It now produces nearly all group revenue, so buying it at face value looks favourable to Adroit rather than extractive. The promoter-group share sales to Abakkus and others at Rs 90 in August 2026 were done by promoter-group companies, not the listed entity, so they are not related-party transactions of Adroit (S28).

The Signet investment and trading ties are the main related-party issue. They tie up about 17% of net worth in a promoter-influenced company outside the core business, and the DRHP-stage sources give no plan to exit it (S14).

items: 46 statutory forms and returns were filed late with the Registrar of Companies, with delays of 1 to 3,771 days. The longest was an MGT-14 for the managing director's 2015-2020 reappointment, due October 2015 and filed February 2026, just before the DRHP (S19).
An RBI compounding application for FEMA procedural lapses at the Canadian subsidiary (late UIN and Foreign Liabilities and Assets reporting) was filed on 17 August 2026 and is still pending (S19).

Two suo motu ROC adjudication applications are pending: one on a company secretary vacancy and one on historical buy-back procedures (S19). The RHP also discloses delays in paying statutory dues (S6).

SEBI refused on 4 March 2026 to exempt the company from classifying the Yashwant Sangla Group as promoter group. Yashwant Sangla, an immediate relative of the promoters, did not provide the required confirmations. Adroit could identify his group's entities only through public-domain searches. It found 14, most of them struck off or dissolved (S11). SEBI had earlier fined Yashwant Sangla, among others, for disclosure lapses in the Linkson International matter (S29).

Litigation against promoters: five criminal matters naming Mukesh Sangla, mostly tied to Signet Industries (a cheque dishonour, a factory safety case, contractor and wage disputes, and an old excise matter), plus an income-tax penalty appeal for AY2010-11 (S20). The DRHP puts promoter litigation at Rs 4.81 cr in aggregate (S1), and ScanX reports promoter criminal and tax proceedings of Rs 5.06 cr (S7). One summary renders the tax penalty as 'Rs 37.75 crore', but that is inconsistent with these aggregates. We read it as about Rs 37.75 million (S20).

Company-level litigation is small: 23 direct-tax matters against the company (Rs 1.66 cr) and 6 against the subsidiary (Rs 2.59 cr), with no criminal cases against the company. The auditors did not qualify any of the restated accounts (S1, S20).

blocks.text: Taken together this is a weak governance record. No single item is disastrous, but compliance was neglected for years and cleaned up only for the IPO, a relative would not cooperate with SEBI disclosure, the promoter faces legal cases, and capital is tied up in a group company. Retail minority shareholders should give this real weight.

items: US tariff and demand exposure. The US took Rs 65.18 cr of FY26 product sales (51.28% of the total). Since 3 May 2025, US shipments of propeller shafts and driveline components carry an additional 25% Section 232 tariff, and a proposed preferential tariff-rate quota has not been implemented (S15).

Unhedged currency exposure. There was no hedging in FY24-FY26 and no formal hedging policy. FX moved from a Rs 5.38 cr loss (FY24) to a Rs 0.50 cr gain (FY26), large relative to PAT of Rs 14-26 cr (S15).
Customer and channel concentration. The top 10 customers were 60.86% of FY26 product sales and the largest one 20.92%. Distributors were 62.45%, and all sales are on purchase orders (S1, S18).
Supplier concentration. The top 10 suppliers accounted for about 90% of purchases (S1).
Single-state manufacturing. All three plants are in Madhya Pradesh (S1).

blocks.text: The tariff risk is the most immediate of these. US revenue has already fallen in absolute terms since FY24 (S9). If the 25% duty continues, Adroit either absorbs the cost through lower margins or loses volume to US or tariff-exempt suppliers.

items: Expansion execution. The plan doubles Pithampur capacity while it runs at 74.70%. Machinery quotes are not binding contracts, and spending runs to FY28 (S17).

Governance and compliance. The record includes 46 late filings, a pending FEMA compounding application, pending ROC adjudications, criminal and tax cases against a promoter, and the undisclosed Yashwant Sangla group interests (S11, S19, S20).
Related-party capital allocation. Rs 21.49 cr is invested in Signet Industries and there is recurring trade with it (S14).
Automotive and EV transition. 74.54% of FY26 product sales come from automotive applications, and electrification reduces propeller shaft content in some vehicle types (S7, S18).

blocks.text: Not included here: generic boilerplate from the RHP such as pandemic risk and general market volatility. The risks listed above are the ones specific to Adroit that could actually change the investment decision.

The DRHP's stated strategy covers expanding manufacturing capacity and automation, growing in North America, engaging OEM customers more directly, digitalisation and advanced manufacturing, and extending the product range toward higher-value offerings (S1). CMD Saurabh Sangla's launch statement called the IPO 'a new phase for the Company', and pointed to vertical integration and a catalogue of more than 5,000 SKUs sold in over 32 countries (S27). He said the focus will be on strengthening capacity, improving efficiency, deepening engagement with distributors, OEMs and Tier-1 customers in export and domestic markets, and broadening automotive and non-automotive applications (S30).

The only concrete, dated commitments we found are the capex schedule (Rs 30.50 cr in FY27 and Rs 33.36 cr in FY28) and the capacity targets of 5,500 MT at Dewas and 18 lakh units at Pithampur (S17). We found no revenue guidance, margin target, order book figure or disclosed customer wins in the sources we could access, and no investor call or detailed interview. We are not inferring an outlook from past trends.

Our reading: management has described its direction but not quantified growth. Given roughly 5% annual growth in product sales and a 25% tariff on the largest market, shareholders have to trust that the doubled capacity will be filled.

items: Quarterly revenue growth, with US and non-US sales separated, and whether growth moves clearly above the FY25-FY26 rate of 4-8% (S3, S15).
EBITDA margin without the FX effect, to see whether about 27.7% holds without currency gains (S3, S15).
Pithampur and Dewas capex spending against the FY27-FY28 schedule (S17).
Any change to the Signet Industries investment, and the result of the FEMA compounding application (S14, S19).
Progress on the stated goal of more direct OEM business. OEMs were only 4.68% of FY26 sales (S18).

subsections.title: Day-1 status, anchors and grey market

blocks.text: This report was written on 23 September 2026, the first day of bidding. At our last check, trackers still showed 0x subscription in every category and were awaiting the first exchange data (S26). No category-wise figures (QIB, NII, retail) were available, so we cannot draw any conclusion about demand yet. QIB and NII bids typically arrive on the last day.

The anchor book opened on 22 September 2026 (S27). Despite several searches, we found no published list of anchor investors, allocation amounts or lock-in details, so we report none. Before the IPO, Abakkus Venture Opportunities Fund (3.18%) and Chattisgarh Investments (0.64%) bought shares from promoter-group companies at Rs 90 (S28). Those were secondary purchases, not anchor bids.

blocks.caption: Grey market premium, unofficial and not an investment signal

blocks.text: The grey market premium is unregulated, thinly traded and easy to move. It fell from Rs 37 to Rs 32 in the days before opening (S25). We ignore it in the verdict.

method: Primary source: the SEBI-hosted Draft Abridged Prospectus (S1, linked from the SEBI filing page S2), which summarises the DRHP dated 30 March 2026. We read it page by page for the business description, product mix, customer and supplier concentration, promoters, objects (DRHP amounts), restated FY23-FY25 and H1 FY26 financials and KPIs, top-10 risk factors, board and litigation summary. The full RHP (company website PDF) was over 10 MB and could not be fetched with our tools, and the NSE-hosted DRHP timed out. RHP-stage data (FY26 restated figures, final objects amounts, FY26 channel, geography, tariff, FX, capacity, RPT, compliance and litigation details) therefore comes from secondary summaries of the RHP. Where possible we cross-checked each figure across at least two of them: Chittorgarh, Novelty Wealth, ScanX, HDFC Sky, Kotak Neo, Groww, Zerodha, IndiaIPO and a series of Multibagg RHP-extract articles. FY24 and FY25 figures in those summaries match the DRHP. Known conflicts and how we handled them: 'total borrowing' figures differ between sources, so we used the DRHP total-debt series and the 0.41x FY26 debt/equity; 5paisa's 'FY26 revenue Rs 127.1 cr' is product sales, not revenue from operations; one source's 'Rs 37.75 crore' tax penalty conflicts with litigation aggregates and was read as Rs 37.75 million; the GCP versus offer-expense split and the make-up of about Rs 12.8 cr of non-product operating revenue could not be confirmed. Some Multibagg extracts go only to the RHP, not the underlying pages, so exact RHP page references could not be checked. No anchor allocation list and no day-1 category subscription data were published at the time of writing. GMP is shown only as unofficial context. Valuation (P/E, EV/EBITDA, peer multiples) is excluded by design, and peer figures are shown only as revenue scale. For web pages without a visible publication date, the date shown is the access date (2026-09-23) or the issue-announcement date.
